title: What happens if a Kafka broker runs out of disk space?
shortTitle: What happens if a Kafka broker runs out of disk space?

s1_definition.profdef: When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker cannot append new records or write index entries, so it logs IO errors, marks the affected log directory offline, and the partitions whose leaders are on that broker become unavailable for writes. Producers to those partitions fail or block, replication stalls so those partitions can fall out of the in-sync replica set, and if the whole broker is affected it may shut down. You prevent and recover from this with retention and cleanup policies, disk monitoring and alerts, quotas, adding capacity or brokers, and in modern versions tiered storage to keep local disk small.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the clerk's desk at National Bank of India is completely covered in ledgers with no room left to write. The clerk cannot record any new transaction, so new entries get rejected and pile up at the counter. The backup clerks who copy the ledgers also cannot keep up, so their copies fall behind. The fix is to archive old ledgers off the desk regularly, watch the desk's fullness and get warned before it overflows, and get a bigger desk or more clerks before the rush.
s1_definition.oneliner: A full broker disk takes its partitions offline for writes and stalls replication, so you prevent it with retention, monitoring, quotas, and capacity, and recover by freeing space or adding disk.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker cannot append new records or write index entries, so it logs IO errors, marks the affected log directory offline, and the partitions whose leaders are on that broker become unavailable for writes. Producers to those partitions fail or block, replication stalls so those partitions can fall out of the in-sync replica set, and if the whole broker is affected it may shut down. You prevent and recover from this with retention and cleanup policies, disk monitoring and alerts, quotas, adding capacity or brokers, and in modern versions tiered storage to keep local disk small.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the clerk's desk at National Bank of India is completely covered in ledgers with no room left to write. The clerk cannot record any new transaction, so new entries get rejected and pile up at the counter. The backup clerks who copy the ledgers also cannot keep up, so their copies fall behind. The fix is to archive old ledgers off the desk regularly, watch the desk's fullness and get warned before it overflows, and get a bigger desk or more clerks before the rush.

**One line to remember:** A full broker disk takes its partitions offline for writes and stalls replication, so you prevent it with retention, monitoring, quotas, and capacity, and recover by freeing space or adding disk.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka stores each partition replica as log segment files plus index files in a configured log directory on local disk. When that directory's filesystem runs out of space, any attempt to append a record or extend an index fails with an IO exception. Kafka treats IO errors on a log directory seriously: it marks that log directory offline, takes the partitions hosted there out of service on that broker, and may shut the broker down if it cannot function.

For the partitions whose leader was on the full broker, writes fail. Producers trying to send to those partitions get errors such as NotEnoughReplicas or timeouts, and with `acks=all` and a sensible `min.insync.replicas`, a write that cannot be safely replicated is rejected rather than silently lost, which is the safe behaviour. If other brokers hold healthy replicas, Kafka elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas, so the partition can recover on another broker, but only if those replicas were in sync; a replica on the full broker falls behind and drops out of the in-sync set.

Replication is also affected because a follower on the full broker cannot write the data it fetches, so it stops making progress and is removed from the in-sync replica set. This reduces the redundancy of every partition that had a replica there, so a second failure becomes more dangerous. This is why a disk-full condition is not just a local problem; it erodes the durability guarantees across the cluster.

Prevention is mostly about retention and monitoring. You set `retention.ms` or `retention.bytes` per topic so old data is deleted on a schedule, and `log.retention.check.interval.ms` controls how often the cleaner runs. For keyed topics you may use compaction, but note that compaction still needs working space. You monitor disk usage per log directory and alert well before full, commonly at seventy or eighty percent, so operators can act. You can set producer and client quotas to stop a runaway producer from filling disks faster than cleanup frees space.

Recovery, once it happens, means freeing space or adding it. You can reduce retention temporarily so the cleaner deletes more, delete or move data for non-critical topics, add disk capacity to the volume, or add brokers and reassign partitions to spread the load. You must be careful that manual deletion of segment files is risky and best avoided; changing retention and letting Kafka clean up is safer. Once space is available, you bring the log directory back online and the affected replicas catch up and rejoin the in-sync set.

A senior nuance is that tiered storage largely prevents this class of incident for high-retention topics by keeping only recent segments locally, so local disk stays small. Another nuance is to spread partitions and data evenly, because an unbalanced cluster can fill one broker while others are near empty, so you monitor per-broker balance and rebalance proactively. A final nuance is that you should separate the Kafka data volume from the operating-system volume, so a full data disk does not also crash the OS and logging.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a transactions topic. One night a surge, plus a retention misconfiguration, fills one broker's data disk. The platform team needs to understand the impact and respond safely.

Problem 1 — the full broker can no longer append records, so transfers routed to its leader partitions start failing. This is exactly the disk-full behaviour: the log directory goes offline and writes to those partitions fail.

Problem 2 — the follower replicas on that broker fall behind and drop out of the in-sync set, reducing redundancy for several partitions. This is exactly how a disk-full condition erodes durability cluster-wide.

Problem 3 — the team must decide a safe recovery: not manual file deletion, but reducing retention, adding capacity, and rebalancing, while monitoring alerts to prevent recurrence. This is exactly the prevention-and-recovery playbook.

The code will model a disk monitor that classifies a broker's disk state, decides whether writes to its partitions are accepted, simulates a follower dropping out of the in-sync set, and recommends a safe recovery action, logged for the transactions topic.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a broker whose disk usage climbs from fifty-five to one hundred percent.

Step 1 — at fifty-five percent the guard classifies the broker as healthy and writes to its leader partitions are accepted normally.

Step 2 — at seventy-five percent the guard raises a warning, telling operators to clean up or add capacity soon. Writes still succeed, but this is the moment to act.

Step 3 — at ninety-two percent the guard classifies it as critical. Operators should act immediately, for example reducing retention so the cleaner deletes old segments.

Step 4 — at one hundred percent the disk is full. The log directory goes offline, so writes to that broker's leader partitions are rejected, producers see errors, and a new leader is elected from in-sync replicas on healthy brokers if available.

Step 5 — the follower replica on the full broker cannot write fetched data, so it falls out of the in-sync replica set, reducing redundancy for the transactions partitions. The guard logs the safe recovery: reduce retention, add disk or brokers, and reassign partitions, explicitly avoiding manual segment deletion.

```
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 55% → HEALTHY | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 75% → WARNING (clean up / add capacity soon) | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 92% → CRITICAL (act now) | writes ACCEPTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [INFO] broker-2 disk 100% → FULL (log dir offline, partitions unavailable for writes) | writes REJECTED
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [WARNING] Follower on broker-2 fell out of ISR for transactions partitions
2026-10-24 23:00:01 [SEVERE] RECOVERY: reduce retention.ms, add disk/brokers, reassign partitions (do NOT hand-delete segment files)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer → transfers (leader on broker-2)
    │
    ▼
  broker-2 disk usage rising
    ├─ < 70%  HEALTHY    → append OK
    ├─ 70-90% WARNING    → append OK, alert operators
    ├─ 90-100% CRITICAL  → append OK, act now
    └─ 100%   FULL       → log dir OFFLINE
         │                    │
         │                    ├─ leader writes REJECTED (producer errors)
         │                    ├─ new leader elected from ISR on healthy broker
         │                    └─ follower on broker-2 drops out of ISR (less redundancy)
         ▼
  RECOVERY (safe):
    reduce retention.ms → cleaner frees segments
    add disk / add brokers → reassign partitions
    (NEVER hand-delete segment files)
    │
    ▼
  log dir back online → replica catches up → rejoins ISR
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Kafka broker's log directory fills up, the broker can no longer append records or write index files, so it logs IO errors, marks that log directory offline, and takes its hosted partitions out of service. For partitions whose leader was on the full broker, writes fail, and producers using all-acknowledgements with a sensible minimum in-sync replicas get rejected rather than silently losing data, which is the safe behaviour. If healthy in-sync replicas exist on other brokers, Kafka elects a new leader there so the partition can recover.

The damage is not just local. A follower replica on the full broker cannot persist the data it fetches, so it falls out of the in-sync replica set, which reduces the redundancy of every partition that had a replica there and makes a second failure more dangerous. That is why a disk-full condition erodes durability across the whole cluster, not just on one node.

I prevent it mainly with retention and monitoring. I set per-topic retention by time or size so old data is cleaned up on schedule, I monitor disk usage per log directory and alert well before full, usually at seventy or eighty percent, and I use quotas to stop a runaway producer. For recovery I never hand-delete segment files, which is risky; instead I reduce retention so the cleaner frees space, add disk or brokers, and reassign partitions to rebalance, then let the recovered replica catch up and rejoin the in-sync set.

In my National Bank of India project, a surge plus a retention misconfiguration once filled one broker. Transfers to its leader partitions started failing and its followers dropped out of the in-sync set. We recovered safely by temporarily cutting retention and adding capacity, and afterward we hardened the setup by separating the data volume from the operating-system volume, balancing partitions evenly, alerting earlier, and ultimately adopting tiered storage so local disks stayed small for our long-retention topics.
